strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and timely question: whether LLM reports about injected internal states reflect something more than shallow prompt-induced confabulation. The contribution is original in moving beyond behavioral demonstrations to a mechanistic account of detection vs. identification.

The empirical program is broad and technically ambitious. The authors test prompt variants, dialogue/persona variants, training stages, base/instruct/abliterated models, and include Qwen3-235B and OLMo-3.1-32B checks in addition to the main Gemma3-27B experiments.

The paper provides multiple causal interventions rather than only correlational probes: projection/residual swaps, bidirectional steering, layer ablation/patching, gate-feature ablation/patching, evidence-carrier interventions, and a learned steering-vector intervention. This substantially strengthens the soundness of the mechanistic claims.

The distinction between detection and identification is well motivated. The authors correctly note that identifying an injected concept may be a relatively direct readout of the added vector, whereas detecting whether an injection occurred is the more interesting behavior.

The paper is generally clearly written, with useful figures, explicit prompts, judge prompts, concept-vector construction details, and a serious limitations/ethics discussion. The dual-use risks of introspection-amplifying interventions and the risk of anthropomorphic interpretation are acknowledged.

The learned steering-vector result is striking: large gains on held-out concepts with reported zero FPR suggest that the default elicitation leaves substantial capability unused, even if the interpretation of this intervention needs caution.
weaknesses: The central terminology and framing remain somewhat stronger than the evidence supports. The experiments show detection of artificial residual-stream perturbations under a prompt explicitly describing such perturbations; calling this “introspective awareness” or “genuine anomaly detection” risks overstating what has been established about faithful self-reporting of natural internal states.

Most mechanistic claims are concentrated on Gemma3-27B and rely heavily on Gemma Scope transcoders/SAEs. The supporting model checks are useful behaviorally, but the detailed evidence-carrier/gate circuit is not shown to generalize across architectures or independently trained feature dictionaries.

The learned steering-vector intervention is trained directly on target completions of the form “Yes, I detect...” and “No, I do not detect...”. Although held-out concepts are used, the intervention may primarily learn a reporting or response-policy manipulation rather than reveal stronger underlying introspection. Generalization to held-out prompts, unrelated internal states, and stronger confabulation controls is limited.

The behavioral evaluation depends on an LLM judge, but the paper does not report human validation, judge calibration, or sensitivity to alternative judges. Since many responses are nuanced or incoherent under strong steering, judge biases could affect detection/introspection rates and downstream partitions into success/failure concepts.

The “0% FPR” claims are important but should be presented with more explicit denominators and uncertainty throughout. Zero observed false positives can still leave nontrivial upper confidence bounds, especially for smaller prompt/persona/model-condition subsets.

The feature-selection pipeline involves many choices: top-200 gates by DLA, hundreds of thousands of carriers, thresholds for correlations/attribution, and selected examples. The paper includes many controls, but multiple-testing and researcher degrees of freedom remain a concern for the strongest feature-level causal story.

Reproducibility is only partially satisfactory. The manuscript says code is available at a blank location, which is a concrete omission. Reproducing the full study also requires large models, expensive sampling, LLM judging, and external transcoder artifacts, so exact reproduction will be difficult without a complete release of code, concept lists, generations, judge outputs, and intervention scripts.

The treatment of attention is less resolved than the MLP story. The paper acknowledges that no individual head is critical while attention may collectively propagate signal, but the main mechanistic narrative may understate this unresolved component.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important and timely question: whether LLM self-reports about injected internal perturbations reflect anything more than shallow prompt compliance or concept leakage.

The paper is unusually extensive for this topic, combining behavioral stress tests, layer sweeps, causal patching/ablation, feature-level analyses with Gemma Scope transcoders, and a learned steering-vector intervention.

Several results are genuinely interesting within the controlled thought-injection setup: base models fail to discriminate injected from control trials, post-trained models show lower false positives, detection and identification peak at different layers, and the single-direction explanation is probed with projection/residual swaps and bidirectional steering tests.

The appendices include full task and judge prompts, concept-vector extraction details, sample sizes for many experiments, and additional analyses across OLMo training stages, abliterated models, and alternative feature/gate choices.

The limitations and broader-impact sections acknowledge important caveats, including limited model coverage, reliance on LLM judges, possible anthropomorphism, and dual-use risks from interventions that amplify self-reporting or weaken refusal behavior.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is too strong for the evidence. The paper repeatedly frames the phenomenon as “introspective awareness” and “genuine anomaly detection,” but the experiments mainly show that injected activation vectors can causally alter answer patterns in a task that explicitly tells the model about injected thoughts. This does not establish faithful introspection in the broader sense suggested by the title and discussion.

Robustness is overstated. Most mechanistic evidence is concentrated on Gemma3-27B, with Qwen3-235B used only for prompt-variant behavior and OLMo showing very weak final instruct performance. The claimed mechanism may be highly model-, prompt-, and artifact-specific.

The behavioral evaluation relies heavily on an LLM judge, with no reported human validation, inter-rater agreement, calibration set, or sensitivity analysis over judge model/prompt. Since small wording differences determine detection, identification, and false-positive rates, this is a significant evidential weakness.

The 0% false-positive claims are rhetorically prominent but not treated with enough statistical care. The manuscript should report exact denominators and confidence intervals wherever it claims zero FPR, and should test harder controls beyond no-injection trials under the same highly suggestive prompt.

The learned steering-vector result is not very convincing as evidence of latent introspective capacity. It is trained directly on targets of the form “Yes, I detect an injected thought about...” versus “No...”, and Appendix N finds a generic YES/affirmation direction. The improvement may largely reflect shifting response priors rather than amplifying a faithful self-monitoring mechanism.

The mechanistic story is plausible but not fully pinned down. Feature labels are LLM-generated, many “gate” and “carrier” features correspond to generic yes/no discourse tokens, and patching/ablation results provide partial causal evidence but do not rule out that the circuit is mainly a response-format or answer-prior circuit rather than an introspection circuit.

The post-training conclusion is underdetermined. Differences between base and instruct checkpoints may reflect chat-format competence, refusal behavior, answer calibration, or judge-compatible response style rather than installation of a specific introspective circuit.

The concept-vector construction introduces confounds. Vectors are derived from “Tell me about {concept}” prompts and are easier to detect for verbalizable, concrete, factual concepts; the paper notes this correlation but still leans on stronger claims about anomaly detection rather than concept salience or decodability.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the reproducibility statement says “all experimental code is available at” but the URL/path is missing in the extracted manuscript. Given the complexity of activation interventions, transcoders, LLM judging, and steering-vector training, this is a material problem.

The ethics section is reasonable but does not quantify the safety side effects of refusal ablation or learned steering. Since the paper explicitly modifies refusal-related behavior and evaluates harmful prompts only briefly in an appendix, stronger safety auditing would be expected.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely mechanistic question: whether apparent LLM self-reports about injected internal states reflect a nontrivial internal computation rather than a shallow yes-bias or prompt artifact. The distinction between detection and identification is well motivated and helps isolate the more interesting part of the phenomenon.

The empirical program is unusually broad for a mechanistic interpretability paper. The authors test prompt variants, dialogue/persona variants, base/instruct/abliterated checkpoints, OLMo training stages, injection-layer sweeps, activation patching, feature ablations, and a learned steering intervention. This gives the main claims considerably more support than a single behavioral demonstration would.

The mechanistic evidence is a major strength. The paper identifies late-layer gate features and earlier evidence-carrier features, tests necessity and partial sufficiency through ablation/patching, and connects the circuit to post-training. The single-linear-direction concern is also addressed thoughtfully through projection/residual swaps and bidirectional steering experiments.

The work is clearly presented despite substantial technical detail. The figures generally communicate the story well, the appendices include prompts, judge prompts, regression/CV details, additional ablations, and attribution analyses, and the limitations section is appropriately candid about model-family dependence, LLM-judge bias, and unresolved attention mechanisms.

The contribution is original and significant for mechanistic interpretability and model self-knowledge research: it moves beyond asking whether introspective behavior exists toward a concrete causal account of how one such behavior may be implemented and elicited.
weaknesses: The central terminology remains somewhat stronger than the evidence. The experiments support internally grounded detection of artificial steering perturbations, but the phrase 'introspective awareness' risks overclaiming relative to what is shown. The authors do note this caveat, but the main framing could more consistently distinguish behavioral/mechanistic self-report from broader introspection.

Most of the mechanistic conclusions rest on Gemma3-27B because the required transcoders are available there. Qwen and OLMo provide useful supporting evidence, but the detailed circuit story may be model-specific. This limits the generality of claims about post-training installing introspective circuitry.

The evaluation pipeline depends heavily on an LLM judge for detection and identification labels. The appendix provides judge prompts, but there is no substantial validation against human labels or inter-judge agreement, so systematic judge bias could affect reported TPR/FPR, success/failure partitions, and downstream analyses.

The phenomenon is demonstrated for a highly artificial intervention: adding concept steering vectors after explicitly telling the model such injections may occur. This is a legitimate controlled setup, but the paper could be clearer about how far the results do or do not transfer to ordinary internal states such as uncertainty, deception, goals, or hidden reasoning.

The causal feature story is persuasive but still partly exploratory. Feature selection uses correlations, direct logit attribution, and post hoc labels, and many evidence-carrier effects are individually weak. The paper would be stronger with more preregistered-style held-out circuit validation, especially for gates/carriers selected on one concept subset and tested on another.

Reproducibility is mostly good in terms of methodological detail, but the reproducibility statement appears to say 'code is available at' without an actual URL in the manuscript text I inspected. For a paper of this complexity, complete code and concept lists are important for acceptance-level reproducibility.

strengths: Timely and original mechanistic study of concept-injection introspection, moving beyond behavioral demonstrations to causal localization, training-stage comparisons, and feature-level circuit hypotheses.

The paper is unusually thorough empirically: it tests prompt variants, persona/chat formats, base/SFT/DPO/instruct checkpoints, refusal ablation, multiple model families for some claims, and held-out concepts for the learned bias vector.

The evidence against the simplest confounds is fairly strong. Projection/residual swaps, bidirectional steering, layer localization, and gate/evidence-carrier interventions all support the claim that detection is not just a single generic affirmative-response direction.

The distinction between detection and identification is conceptually useful and supported by layer sweeps and forced-identification experiments, making the contribution more precise than a broad claim that models are simply 'introspective'.

The limitations and ethics sections are unusually candid, including the artificiality of the setup, reliance on LLM judges, limited model coverage, dual-use risks, and the fact that the learned bias vector degrades chain-of-thought faithfulness and prefill detection.
weaknesses: The central framing still risks overclaiming: the experiments demonstrate detection of injected activation perturbations in a highly artificial prompt/task, but the term 'introspective awareness' may suggest broader self-knowledge than the evidence supports. The paper acknowledges this, but the abstract and discussion sometimes lean stronger than warranted.

Most mechanistic conclusions rely heavily on Gemma3-27B and Gemma Scope transcoders. Supporting behavioral results on Qwen and OLMo help, but the claimed two-stage circuit is not shown to generalize mechanistically across model families.

The behavioral labels depend on GPT-4.1-mini judging, yet the manuscript does not appear to report human validation, judge agreement, or sensitivity to alternative judges. Since small changes in detection/FPR are important, this is a material reproducibility and soundness concern.

Some causal evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. The gate/evidence-carrier story depends on transcoder feature interpretations and interventions, but evidence carriers are individually weak, attention remains unclear, and the circuit may be an incomplete abstraction of a more distributed computation.

The post-training claim is interesting but not fully pinned down. DPO and contrastive losses correlate with lower FPR and some above-chance detection, but the mechanism by which preference training induces this behavior is not identified, and some reported LoRA effects are modest.

Reproducibility is generally well documented in prompts and hyperparameters, but the reproducibility statement says code is available at a blank location, which is a concrete issue for an ICML submission. Several results also require substantial compute and external large-model/transcoder artifacts.

The learned bias-vector result is double-edged: it boosts the benchmark but appears to induce a shorter, more assertive reporting mode and worsens CoT faithfulness and prefill detection, limiting its interpretation as a genuine improvement in introspective capability.

strengths: The manuscript studies an interesting and timely phenomenon: whether open-weight LLMs can report activation steering interventions, and it goes beyond behavioral replication by attempting mechanistic localization.

The experimental scope is substantial: prompt variants, dialogue-format variants, base/SFT/DPO/instruct checkpoints, refusal-direction ablation, learned bias vectors, and several appendices with additional checks.

The paper usefully distinguishes detection from identification and shows evidence that these peak in different layers, which is a meaningful observation for future work on concept injection and self-report.

The authors are fairly candid about some limitations, including the artificiality of the setup, reliance on LLM judges, limited model coverage for mechanistic analyses, unclear role of attention, and lack of evidence for broader self-knowledge transfer.

The downstream analysis of the learned bias vector is a strength: it shows negligible transfer to hallucination detection and degradation in CoT faithfulness and prefill detection, tempering the strongest interpretation of the intervention.
weaknesses: The central framing as “introspective awareness” remains under-supported. The main prompt explicitly tells the model that an injection may occur, calls it a “thought,” and asks for a yes/no report; this makes it difficult to separate genuine internal-state access from prompt-conditioned reporting, anomaly response, or learned discourse patterns.

The false-positive story is fragile. The claimed 0% FPR is computed over trial numbers 1-10, while the appendix notes that other trial numbers such as “Trial 30” can systematically induce confabulation. This substantially weakens the behavioral robustness claim.

The controls do not fully rule out shallow steering artifacts. The paper discusses generic yes-bias and includes some geometric tests, but many identified “gate” and “carrier” features are directly related to yes/no answer boundaries, discourse transitions, emphatic responses, or factual/assertive style, so the mechanistic account may partly redescribe response-style control rather than establish introspection.

The mechanistic claims are stronger than the causal evidence warrants. Feature selection is heavily guided by direct logit attribution to Yes-No behavior, and some reported causal effects are partial or modest; evidence carriers number in the hundreds of thousands and individual interventions are weak, making the proposed two-stage circuit somewhat diffuse.

The post-training conclusion is suggestive but not decisive. DPO effects are small in several settings, evaluated on limited concept sets for some checkpoints, and may reflect changes in calibration/refusal/answer style rather than emergence of a specific introspective mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many details: the manuscript says “all experimental code is available at” but the URL is blank, and key components such as full concept lists, generated outputs, judge decisions, trained vectors/adapters, and intervention scripts are essential for verifying the claims.

The paper relies heavily on LLM judges without reporting human validation, inter-rater checks, judge sensitivity analyses, or robustness to judge model choice. This is important because the outcome labels are subtle and can be affected by phrasing and coherence filters.

The learned bias vector result is over-interpretable as amplified introspection. The authors’ own downstream experiments show it induces shorter, more assertive reporting and worsens prefill detection and CoT faithfulness, which supports a narrower interpretation: it improves this benchmark by changing response style rather than reliably improving self-knowledge.

Presentation is often confident beyond the evidence. Phrases such as “trace a causal pathway” and “mechanistically nontrivial introspective awareness” should be softened given the artificial task, prompt leakage, selected feature analyses, and unresolved confounds.

Ethics discussion is present but shallow relative to the claims: the work studies model awareness of interventions and methods that reduce refusal behavior, yet safety evaluation is limited and the abliterated model procedure intentionally optimizes refusal bypass on harmful prompts.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: whether apparent LLM introspective awareness under concept-vector injection is mechanistically grounded or a shallow prompting/steering artifact. The contribution is significant for mechanistic interpretability and model self-report reliability.

The empirical program is unusually broad. The authors evaluate prompt variants, dialogue/persona variants, base/SFT/DPO/instruct checkpoints, refusal-direction ablation, direction-swap tests, bidirectional steering, per-layer causal interventions, transcoder feature interventions, and a held-out-concept learned bias-vector experiment.

The core claims are supported by multiple converging lines of evidence. In particular, the paper makes a convincing case that detection is not simply a generic affirmative-answer direction: projection/residual swaps both matter, opposite directions can both induce detection for success-success pairs, and positive direct-logit 'Yes' features do not have the same causal effect as the proposed gate features.

The mechanistic analysis is one of the strongest parts of the paper. The evidence-carrier/gate account is supported by causal ablation and patching, layer localization around the L45 MLP, replication across several gate features, comparison with base and abliterated models, and feature-level attribution graphs.

The paper is well written and well organized despite its complexity. The distinction between detection, forced identification, and full introspection is clear, and the authors appropriately emphasize that detection is the more mechanistically interesting component.

Reproducibility is above average for this kind of work: the manuscript includes full task and judge prompts, concept-vector construction, trial structure, DPO/LoRA hyperparameters, cross-validation details, transcoder intervention formulas, and extensive appendix analyses. The limitations and responsible-use discussion are also serious and appropriately scoped.
weaknesses: The central phenomenon is still demonstrated in a highly artificial intervention setting: adding explicit concept vectors and asking the model whether a thought was injected. The paper is careful about this, but the broader language around 'introspective awareness' could still be read as stronger than the evidence warrants for ordinary self-knowledge or faithful reports about natural internal states.

Most mechanistic conclusions rely heavily on Gemma3-27B because of available transcoders. The behavioral phenomenon is checked on Qwen and OLMo, but the detailed circuit account is not independently replicated in another architecture/model family, limiting generality.

The behavioral metrics depend substantially on LLM judges. The appendix gives judge prompts and coherence filters, but the paper would be stronger with human validation or inter-judge robustness, especially because small changes in FPR are important to the claims.

The DPO/post-training conclusion is suggestive but not fully isolated. Official checkpoint comparisons confound many training changes, and the LoRA DPO replications yield modest effects, especially for Gemma relative to the official instruct model. Thus 'contrastive preference training enables introspection' is plausible but not decisively established as the mechanism of emergence.

The feature-level circuit story remains partly post hoc and partial. Evidence carriers are numerous and individually weak, attention is acknowledged as not fully understood, and transcoder feature labels/interpretations depend on imperfect unsupervised artifacts and model-generated labels. The causal interventions are valuable, but they do not yet provide a complete mechanistic proof.

Some headline improvements from the learned bias vector need careful interpretation. Appendix results indicate nontrivial side effects, including shorter/more assertive responses and degraded performance on some broader self-knowledge or faithfulness tasks, so the vector is better viewed as targeted elicitation for this benchmark than as a general introspection improvement.

The manuscript appears to have blank or anonymized code/model links in a few places. Even if this is for review anonymity, acceptance should require that the promised code, concept lists, and trained artifacts are actually released in usable form.
